Chapter Seven: Portrait Drawing—Seeing and Capturing the Human Face
Let’s be honest—portrait drawing has a reputation. It’s often seen as the ultimate test of how closely you can observe. After all, faces are so familiar, yet every one is completely unique—and even a tiny mistake can make a portrait look just a bit... off.
Here’s the trick: instead of seeing a face as a collection of symbols—like eyes, a nose, and a mouth—try looking at it as a set of shapes, spaces, and subtle shifts in light and dark.
It all starts with observation. When you’re drawing, forget about “drawing an eye.” Instead, pay attention to the abstract shapes: the way the eyelids curve, the arch of the brow, and the shadows tucked underneath.
Want to keep everything in proportion? Measure the distances between the features—like the space from the bottom of the nose to the chin. A simple pencil, held out at arm’s length, makes a great measuring stick.
Here are a few gentle guidelines to keep you moving in the right direction:
Start with a loose outline of the head—don’t get caught up in the details just yet.
Use light lines to mark where the main features go, and pay attention to the shapes and spaces between them.
Rather than relying on what you think you remember, really look at the angles and relationships between each feature.
Gradually build up the values—add shading to suggest depth and roundness, letting the face slowly emerge from the paper.
And here’s a handy trick: if you want to check the likeness, try looking at your drawing in a mirror or even upside down. It’s a great way to spot anything that feels off.
Think of the face as a landscape—there are hills like cheekbones, valleys like eye sockets, and rivers formed by lines and wrinkles. When you look at it this way, you’ll notice you start seeing more, and labeling less.
But portrait drawing isn’t just about getting the features right. As you observe all those subtle asymmetries and unique details, you start to see the real person behind the face.
It becomes a process of empathy and connection—both with your subject, and with yourself as an artist.
So, next time you sit down to draw a portrait, try letting go of the idea of perfection. Focus on observation, stay curious, and let yourself connect with the face in front of you. Who knows—you might just discover something new, both on the page and within yourself.
